paras: The lynching of John Risbee and Wyley Lee took place at Chetopa, Kansas, in the early morning of June 27, 1888, when a mob of 200 to 300 men took the two Black men from a sheriff's guard and hanged them from a newspaper office window. The two had been accused of shooting the town marshal and his deputy, both of whom were later reported alive. Papers noted it chiefly for a coroner's jury of four white and eight Black men that split over naming the mob.

According to the Indian Chieftain of nearby Vinita, Risbee had been drunk, riding horseback down sidewalks and into stores, and a warrant was issued for his arrest. Marshal William Bentley failed to arrest him, and Ed Martin was deputized to help. When the officers returned on Tuesday afternoon, Lee had joined Risbee and both officers were shot; the Kansas City wire said the two fired while trying to escape.

Sheriff Wilson tried to take the prisoners to the county jail at Oswego on the midnight train, but crowds told him they must not leave town before a preliminary examination, so he held them under guard in the city hall as armed men came in from the country. At 12:30 a report spread that Martin had died and Bentley was dying, and, in the Parsons correspondent's words, "threats of lynching were freely made."

About 1 o'clock the electric light went out and about 200 men pushed into the city hall, where the sheriff struck one of them with his revolver before his guard was overpowered. The prisoners, handcuffed together, were dragged from under a table, allowed to pray, and taken into the adjoining Chetopa Statesman office. With ropes tied to timbers and around their necks, they were made to jump from an upper window about 2 a.m.; Risbee's neck broke and Lee strangled. The coroner cut the bodies down at 9 o'clock, and hundreds visited the scene.

The coroner's jury, four white and eight Black citizens, deadlocked: the white jurors wanted a verdict of death "at the hands of parties unknown," while the Black jurors said over one hundred of the mob were known and refused to agree unless they were charged. Separate majority and minority verdicts were expected; no report of a final verdict, arrests or prosecution was found.

A week later the Indian Chieftain wrote that both officers were alive with hopes of recovery. The Wichita Eagle said the death report had been spread "with the evident purpose of infuriating the mob" and that Chetopa was "in a condition of mutiny," with white citizens armed against expected Black retaliation.

The story spread chiefly through a Kansas City wire on four Kansas lynchings, which the New York Sun subheaded "The Citizens Disgusted by the Law's Leniency Toward Murderers" and blamed on the state's unenforced death penalty. Shorter versions ending "No legal hangings occur in Kansas" ran from Connecticut to Dakota, garbling Risbee's name. The Maysville, Kentucky, Evening Bulletin headed the Parsons account "A Trio of Murderers Meet With Justice," and a pre-lynching item titled "A Bad Negro's Work" had said the prospects of a lynching were good.

The coroner's-jury dispute ran under headlines such as "On the Color Line" and "A Jury Divided on Race Lines" in Washington, Wheeling, Louisville and Ohio papers. The Savannah Morning News called the men murderers but editorialized that "the colored jurors were in the right." A Missouri weekly used the lynching to needle "the good republican state of Kansas", a South Carolina paper reprinted the Iowa Citizen calling the week's Kansas lynchings a "damnable outrage," and a December list of the year's lynchings included the case.

Pre-lynching state news named the man who rode into a store and fought the officers as James Riley or "One-eyed" Riley, with details matching the Vinita account of Risbee. Early reports said Martin was fatally wounded, and one brief said the two "murdered" Marshal Bently, but later Vinita and Wichita reports said both officers survived. Most reports put the hanging on Tuesday night or early Wednesday, but some June 28 dispatches said "this morning" and a Missouri weekly said Thursday.

accounts.label: Parsons dispatch
accounts.gist: The men were arrested for shooting the marshal and deputy; a crowd kept the sheriff from moving them; after a false report of Martin's death, about 200 men stormed the city hall, let them pray, and hanged them from the Statesman office window at 2 a.m.

accounts.label: Kansas City wire
accounts.gist: The two shot both officers 'in making a desperate attempt to escape'; a mob of 300 overpowered the guard after the light went out and forced them to jump at gunpoint.

accounts.label: Indian Chieftain (Vinita)
accounts.gist: Risby, drunk, resisted a warrant; when two officers came, Lee joined him and both officers were shot; a masked mob took them from the guard; a week later the paper reported both officers alive.

accounts.label: Pre-lynching state news
accounts.gist: A 'desperate negro' named James Riley or 'One-eyed' Riley, drunk, rode into a store, beat Marshal Bentley, and with a companion fired on the officers, fatally wounding Martin.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: White jurors wanted 'parties unknown'; colored jurors said over a hundred of the mob were known and wanted them charged.

framing.detail: The Maysville Evening Bulletin headed the Parsons dispatch 'A Trio of Murderers Meet With Justice at the Hands of Kansas Mobs'.

The Sun's 'Four Lynchings in Kansas' was subheaded 'The Citizens Disgusted by the Law's Leniency Toward Murderers' and blamed Kansas's unenforced death penalty, while calling the victims' lives 'wretched'.
A pre-lynching item titled 'A Bad Negro's Work' said 'the prospects of a lynching are good'.
The Savannah Morning News editorial 'Mob Law in Kansas' held the men guilty of murder but said the colored jurors were right and the lynchers should be named.
The Butler (Mo.) Weekly Times used the lynching for a partisan jab at Republican Kansas, noting it would have been a campaign document had it happened in South Carolina.
Coroner's-jury dispatches ran under 'On the Color Line' and 'A Jury Divided on Race Lines'.
The Wichita Eagle said the false report of the deputy's death was circulated to infuriate the mob.
The Abbeville Press and Banner reprinted the Iowa Citizen calling the week's Kansas lynchings 'a damnable outrage'.

conflicts.note: The Indian Chieftain of Thursday June 28 already reported the hanging as 'Tuesday night', which supports early Wednesday June 27.

The Riley stories describe the same drunken ride into a store, warrant, beating of Bentley and shooting with a companion that the Indian Chieftain attributes to Risby; no paper says a third man was killed.

From an upper-story window of the Chetopa Statesman printing office, next to the city hall, Chetopa
John Risbee (also printed Risby, Kisbee, Bisbee, Hisbee, Rishee, Risboe) and Wyley Lee (also Wylie, Wiley), described as 'negroes' and 'colored men'
Accused of shooting City Marshal William Bentley and Deputy Ed Martin while resisting arrest on a warrant for drunken disorder (or, in the wire version, while trying to escape)
A mob of Chetopa citizens, joined by men from the country armed with shotguns; masked, per the Indian Chieftain
Later reports said both officers were alive with hope of recovery; the report of Martin's death that preceded the lynching was untrue
